newsitem.title: CHINA: Rain eases drought in N.China but worst not over.
newsitem.headline: Rain eases drought in N.China but worst not over.

text.p: Rains in parts of northern and northeastern China have helped to ease a drought threatening the autumn grain harvest but the worst was not over, the China Daily said on Tuesday.

Rains averaging 25-50 mm between July 27 and August 2 could reduce the possibility of severe crop failure in some provinces and had caused flooding along the Yellow River, which had dried up in some sections for up to 131 days, it quoted officials as saying.
The river flow could resume on some reaches of the river by Thursday, it quoted officials of the State Flood Control and Drought Prevention Headquarters as saying.

However, the drought, which has affected a record 20 million hectares of crops and farmland across China, was still threatening more than 8.3 million hectares. Of that total, 40 percent were severely affected and 16 percent of that was dying, it said.
"The worst of the year's severe drought is not over yet," it quoted an official from the Ministry of Agriculture as saying.
In eastern Shandong province and parts of northeastern Hebei province, two of China's main grain producing areas, the drought was worsening after no rain last week, it said.

In Shandong's capital, Jinan, the heatwave had caused the city's water table to drop to only 24 metres, three metres lower than in the same period last year, and water shortages were affecting 30 percent of the city's population, it said.
The Yellow River Water Plant which normally supplied 200,000 cubic metres of water daily had suspended operations because of low water levels on the lower reaches, it said.
Officials had said they hoped typhoons that hit southern and eastern coastal provinces last weekend would help to ease the drought in the north in ensuing weeks, it said.
China gathers more than 70 percent of its total annual grain crop in the autumn harvest.

Officials have said the drought was expected to cut the size of China's corn harvest this year, although overall grain production was expected to be about 484 million tonnes, only slightly below last year's record 490 million tonnes.
While drought and high temperatures have been plaguing northern China, floods have wrought havoc in the south.
